Motivated by fast matrix multiplication and recent connections between asymptotic tensor rank and fine-grained complexity, we revisit classical tools from the matrix multiplication literature and develop a framework for obtaining improved asymptotic rank upper bounds for tensors beyond matrix multiplication.
In the 1980s, Coppersmith-Winograd and Strassen discovered a series of speedup theorems for asymptotic rank: in certain regimes, one can extract additional terms from a border rank upper bound on a tensor T, and then use these terms to obtain an improved asymptotic rank of T. We establish general speedup theorems that subsume these results and enable quantitative improvements. Two representative applications are:  
1) The asymptotic rank of the small Coppersmith-Winograd tensor cw_q is less than its border rank. For instance, we prove ̰{R}(cw₂) < 3.931, improving on ̲{R}(cw₂) = 4. It is known that ̰{R}(cw₂) = 3 would imply ω = 2. 
2) A general improvement over Strassen’s bound: we obtain an upper bound below d^{2ω/3} on the asymptotic rank of any d× d× d tensor.  To make full use of speedups, we analyze degenerations in which both sides are nontrivial direct sums, a setting where the optimal quantitative bound one can achieve was previously unclear.  1      Introduction
The exponent of matrix multiplication, ω, is defined as the smallest real number such that
two n ˆ n matrices can be multiplied using at most nω`op1q field operations. Because of the
fundamental and widespread applications of matrix multiplication algorithms, determining
the value of ω has become one of the most important open problems in computer science.
Strassen’s famous algorithm [43] showed the first nontrivial bound ω ď log2 p7q ă 2.81. Since
then, a long line of follow-up work has culminated in the current best bound ω ă 2.371339 [2].
The only known lower bound is the straightforward ω ě 2, since the input and output sizes
are n2 . In fact, it is frequently conjectured that ω “ 2.
    It has been known since Strassen’s work [44] that determining ω is equivalent to under-
standing the asymptotic rank of the matrix multiplication tensor. In fact, there are three
different rank notions for a (3-mode/3-dimensional) tensor T which have played a prominent

          More recently, the asymptotic rank of tensors has found other algorithmic applications

sum inequality is never tight: One always has the strict inequality ω ă 3τ ! Their proof is
constructive, in the sense that they found a systematic way to convert a given direct sum

   This type of result is reminiscent of Blum’s classical speedup theorem for Turing ma-
chines [13], and so we refer to such results as speedup theorems in this paper. That said,
Blum’s speedup theorem concerns non-constructible time functions, whereas the tensor
speedup theorems we discuss here concern explicit problems of great interest like matrix
multiplication.

Our approach. In this paper, we revisit the approach of bounding the asymptotic ranks of
tensors via speedup theorems. We establish a generalization of prior speedup theorems, and
analyze them using a method we call Strassen calculus which makes use of Strassen’s theory

will discuss this in much more detail in Section 2 below, but we first present some applications
of our approach.

       2.1    Strassen calculus: Bounds via asymptotic spectrum
       Traditionally, techniques for bounding the matrix multiplication exponent ω proceed by

    In Section 4, we introduce Strassen calculus – a systematic framework for deriving bounds
from a fixed collection of degenerations between direct sums of tensors – via Strassen’s theory
of the asymptotic spectrum [41, 42, 46].
    Informally, the asymptotic spectrum provides a family of numerical “measures” for tensors.
Concretely, an element of the asymptotic spectrum X is a function

   ϕ : tF-tensorsu Ñ Rě0

that behaves well with respect to the tensor operations. We refer to such a function ϕ as a
spectral point; see Section 4 for the precise definitions.
    The key structural statement underlying the theory of the asymptotic spectrum is Strassen
duality (Theorem 6). Roughly speaking, it says that asymptotic degeneration relations
are exactly the relations that hold after applying all spectral points: if T asymptotically
degenerates to S, then ϕpT q ď ϕpSq for every ϕ, and conversely, if this inequality holds for
all ϕ, then this implies the existence of the asymptotic degeneration. In particular, this
characterizes asymptotic rank via a max formula,

   RpT q “ max ϕpT q.
   r       ϕPX

Conceptually, this turns questions about asymptotic rank into optimization problems over
the asymptotic spectrum.
    Of course, the space X of all spectral points is defined nonconstructively and may be
infinite-dimensional a priori, so constructing explicit spectral points is generally difficult,
although there has been significant progress in the past decade [19, 17, 37]. Our approach
is therefore not to “parametrize” X directly. Instead, we start from a fixed collection
of tensor degenerations, translate them into numerical inequalities that must be satisfied
by every spectral point, and then use Strassen duality to turn the resulting constraints
into explicit upper bounds on asymptotic rank. In favorable regimes one can solve the
corresponding optimization problems analytically; more generally, one can obtain sharp
bounds via computer-aided evaluation. Moreover, Strassen calculus is complete: for a fixed

           We emphasize that although the theory of the asymptotic spectrum was originally
       motivated by the study of tensor rank, its subsequent development has followed a curious
       trajectory. While the framework has flourished in other areas such as (quantum) information
       theory, its application to the asymptotic rank of tensors has remained largely conceptual.
       Prior to this work, the theory occupied a somewhat dormant role in its own founding domain,
       as to the best of our knowledge, no practical instances were identified to yield concrete,
       improved upper bounds.
           The following examples illustrate the utility of the framework in other areas, and highlight
       the gap between its success elsewhere and its (so far) limited impact on tensor rank:
           Strassen’s Foundation. In his seminal paper [41], Strassen introduced the asymptotic
           spectrum to provide a new proof of the asymptotic sum inequality, setting the stage for a
           theory that, while foundational, remained difficult to apply to specific new bounds.
           Barriers to Fast Matrix Multiplication. Improvements to the exponent ω over the past
           thirty years have largely relied on analyzing the big Coppersmith–Winograd tensor CWq .
           However, Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam [18] utilized spectral points to show that the
           laser method – even in a highly generalized form – applied on big CW tensors, cannot
           yield an upper bound better than 2.16. Subsequent work [16] has established analogous
           barriers for the rectangular case.
           Graph Theory. Zuiddam [49] applied the general theory of asymptotic spectrum (not
           confined to tensors) to study the Shannon capacity ΘpGq of graphs. Wigderson and
           Zuiddam [47, Theorem 4.1] utilized the asymptotic spectrum to show a striking equivalence:
           for graphs G and H, where G b H and G \ H denote the strong product and disjoint
           union respectively, ΘpG b Hq ą ΘpGqΘpHq if and only if ΘpG \ Hq ą ΘpGq ` ΘpHq.1
           Circuit Complexity. Robere and Zuiddam [35] developed an analogous theory to study
           and generalize some results in the complexity of catalytic branching programs. Alman
           and Li [3] applied asymptotic spectrum theory to derive a duality theorem for depth-2

2.2    Speedup theorems
In Section 5, we prove a general speedup theorem that subsumes the results of Coppersmith–
Winograd [22] and Strassen [41, Theorem 3.14]. The Coppersmith–Winograd theorem fits the
following paradigm: starting from a border rank bound T Ĳ xry, one can (in certain regimes)
“speed up” the degeneration by taking a direct sum with a one-slice matrix multiplication
tensor on both sides, obtaining

   T ‘ x1, t, 1y Ĳ xry ‘ x1, s, 1y.

    Strassen later generalized this by showing that the right-hand side does not necessarily
need to be a diagonal tensor (i.e., a border rank bound). Specifically, a degeneration T Ĳ S
can also be accelerated to T ‘ x1, t, 1y Ĳ S ‘ x1, s, 1y. Our main theorem further generalizes
this idea: under suitable hypotheses, it allows one to add arbitrary tensors on both sides of a
degeneration, producing relations of the form T ‘ T 1 Ĳ S ‘ S 1 .
    In Section 6, we present three concrete instantiations of the general speedup theorem.
Each has different strengths and ranges of applicability; together, they form the main toolkit
we use to derive explicit upper bounds on asymptotic rank.
    The first result relates a certain variant of the min-rank problem to one-slice speedups of
    the form T ‘ x1, t, 1y Ĳ S ‘ x1, s, 1y, thereby recovering Strassen’s speedup theorem.
    The second result shows that, in a suitable regime, a degeneration of the form T ‘x1, t, 1y Ĳ
    S 1 can be further accelerated to T ‘ x1, t1 , 1y Ĳ S 1 for some t1 ą t, while keeping the
    right-hand side fixed. In particular, if one takes an identity obtained from the first result
    and takes a tensor power of both sides, this acceleration always applies; thus the first
    method can be iterated. This generalizes a result of Coppersmith and Winograd [22,
    Theorem B].
    The third result shows that, in a certain regime, one can add multiple one-slice tensors
